topics.title: Nutrition in Plants and Animals
objectives: Student can distinguish autotrophic from heterotrophic nutrition with one everyday example of each.
Student can state the raw materials and products of photosynthesis and build its word equation.
Student can explain what stomata do and why guard cells close them when the plant risks losing too much water.
Student can trace food through the human alimentary canal and name what acts on it at each stop — saliva in the mouth, acid and pepsin in the stomach, intestinal juices in the small intestine.
Student can explain why villi make the small intestine the main site of absorption.
visualIdeas: Leaf cross-section as a box with labelled arrows: CO2 in, O2 out, sunlight from above, water arriving from the roots
Photosynthesis word equation assembled term by term as a formula element
Alimentary canal as a chain of boxes mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine, with a note appearing beside each stop naming its juice or enzyme
Zoom-in box on villi drawn with pen strokes to show how folding multiplies surface area

topics.title: Respiration
objectives: Student can explain why respiration is a cellular process — every cell burns glucose, breathing only supplies the oxygen.
Student can compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration by their end products and the energy each releases.
Student can explain muscle cramps after a sprint using lactic acid build-up, and name what yeast makes instead.
Student can describe how millions of alveoli give the lungs a huge exchange surface and trace oxygen and carbon dioxide across it.
Student can state why ATP is called the energy currency of the cell.
visualIdeas: Glucose box splitting into pyruvate, then three branching arrow paths: with oxygen (CO2 + water + lots of energy), without oxygen in muscle (lactic acid), in yeast (alcohol + CO2)
Sprinter example: run → cramp as a 'bad'-tone note on the lactic acid branch
Lungs box with a zoom-in on one alveolus and a paired set of arrows, O2 in and CO2 out
ATP drawn as a small coin note that reappears whenever energy is spent

topics.title: The Heart and Double Circulation
objectives: Student can name the four chambers of the heart and the receiving job of atria versus the pumping job of ventricles.
Student can trace double circulation — the short lung loop and the long body loop — and explain why blood passes through the heart twice in one full round.
Student can explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right: it must push blood to the whole body, not just the nearby lungs.
Student can compare arteries and veins by wall thickness, blood pressure, valves, and direction of flow.
Student can explain why keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate suits warm-blooded animals with high energy needs.
visualIdeas: Four-chamber grid of boxes RA / LA / RV / LV inside a heart outline
Two arrow loops colour-coded by tone: a short lungs loop and a long body loop, oxygenated legs in 'good' tone
Side-by-side artery vs vein boxes with notes: thick elastic wall under high pressure vs thin wall with valves
Pen stroke thickening the LV wall while the narration explains the pressure difference

topics.title: Blood and Its Components
objectives: Student can name the four components of blood — plasma, red cells, white cells, platelets — and one job of each.
Student can explain why haemoglobin makes red blood cells such efficient oxygen carriers.
Student can describe how platelets plug a cut and start the clot that stops bleeding.
Student can state what lymph is and how it differs from blood.
visualIdeas: Blood in a test-tube box: pale plasma layer on top, cell layer below, labels appearing one by one
Three character boxes with jobs: RBC as delivery van, WBC as security guard, platelet as repair crew
A cut drawn as a pen stroke with platelet arrows converging on it and a 'good'-tone clot note
Dashed arrow leaking plasma out of a capillary to show where lymph comes from

topics.title: Excretion — Kidneys and Nephrons
objectives: Student can explain why the body must remove urea, naming the liver as where it is made and the kidney as where it is filtered out.
Student can trace urine from kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra.
Student can describe filtration and selective reabsorption in a nephron — glucose and most water return to the blood, urea does not.
Student can explain what dialysis does for a patient whose kidneys have failed.
visualIdeas: Body outline with two kidney boxes and ureter arrows running down to a bladder box
Nephron zoom box: blood in, filtrate arrow out, reabsorption arrows returning glucose and water in 'good' tone, urea arrow leaving in 'bad' tone
Dialysis machine as an external box plumbed to the arm with dashed arrows, labelled as an artificial kidney
